blocks.text: Material & CO2 Estimation for 1,082 Buildings – Method and Results
23 September 2026
1. Summary

This document explains how material mass and CO2 were calculated for 1,082 buildings from their 3DBAG and BAG data: 1,081 demolition buildings plus one added building, Jan Provostlaan 16 in Bilthoven. The result is 1,800,610 tonnes of material and 393,535 tonnes CO2e, reported in 7 materials.

Mass is unchanged by the factors; only CO2 moves. Before 23 September 2026 each detailed material had its own factor and the total was 447,580 t CO2e. The factors are now one flat value per reported material group (section 8.7), which gives 393,535 t CO2e, 12% lower. Steel falls most (156,131 → 132,686 t) because reinforcement went from 1.99 to 1.55 kg CO2e per kg; wood and brick rise slightly.
Every number is one of three kinds:
MEASURED – read directly from a BAG or 3DBAG field.
DERIVED – calculated only from measured numbers.
ASSUMED – our own chosen value, used only where 3DBAG cannot tell us (construction build-up, storey height, window share, emission factors).

Where the assumptions are: every assumption has an ID (A1–A19). Section 8.1 is the complete assumption register: value, where it is used, why it is needed and how much it changes the result. In the text and tables, an assumed value is marked [ASSUMED Ax].
Section 12 repeats the whole calculation step by step for one building, so every figure can be checked by hand.

blocks.text: 2.2 Why 1,082 buildings

The source file has 1,187 notices, but some buildings appear in more than one notice. Counting unique pand_id (building ID) gives 1,081 buildings. We keep the same 1,081 notices as the existing estimation file, so each building is counted once; the other 106 notices are left out of the input file. One building without a demolition notice is added: Jan Provostlaan 16, 3723RD Bilthoven (pand_id 0310100000664117, single-family house built 1988, material_profile_id EEN_1970_2000). Its outline and dwelling unit come from the PDOK BAG API and its measured areas and volume from the 3DBAG API – the same fields as for the notices. It has no notice, so its notice_id is manual-0310100000664117. build_input_1082.py writes these 1,082 buildings to 3dbag_input_1082.json, the single input of the calculation.

blocks.text: 3. Method in 7 steps
Assign a build-up profile from building type and age (section 4).
Read the measured fields from 3DBAG and BAG (section 5).
Derive geometry: perimeter, heights, wall lengths (section 6).
Derive floor areas from volume and storey height (section 7).
Calculate component quantities – m² or m of each building part (section 9).
Calculate material mass = quantity × kg per m² of each layer, summed per material (section 10).
Calculate CO2 = mass × emission factor, and group into 7 materials (section 11).
4. Step 1 – Assign a build-up profile

3DBAG tells us sizes, not materials. So each building gets one of 10 build-up profiles, chosen from the first and second part of its material_profile_id. [ASSUMED A10] – the link between building type/age and construction is our own choice.

Meaning

rows: overig (other: assembly, healthcare, hotel, sports, education)

blocks.text: The age part (PRE_1945, 1945_1970, 1970_2000, POST_2000) is kept as it is. Industrial buildings use only two age groups: before 1970 and from 1970.

blocks.text: 5. Step 2 – Measured inputs
For every building these values are read without change. Short symbols used below:

head: Symbol
Field
Unit
rows: sum of oppervlakte_m2 of all dwelling units (usable floor area)

blocks.text: Empty wall or roof areas count as 0. A value of 0 is real: for example opp_scheidingsmuur = 0 means a detached building with no shared wall. [ASSUMED A17] – an empty (null) field is treated as 0.
6. Step 3 – Derived geometry
6.1 Perimeter from the footprint outline
The outline is in degrees. Each corner is converted to metres around the building's own latitude φ (a local flat-earth approximation, accurate to well under 1% at building size) [ASSUMED A19]:
x = (lon − lon₁) × m_lon      y = (lat − lat₁) × m_lat
Each side is then √(Δx² + Δy²) and the perimeter P is the sum of all sides. The outline area follows from the shoelace formula:
A_outline = ½ × | Σ (xᵢ × yᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁ × yᵢ) |
6.2 Outline check and correction
If A_outline differs from opp_grond by more than 2%, the building is flagged.
If it differs by more than 10%, the outline is not this 3DBAG footprint. We keep its shape but scale it to the measured size: P_used = P × √(A_ground ÷ A_outline). [ASSUMED A14]
6.3 Heights (checks)
H_max = h_dak_max − h_maaiveld      H_mean = V ÷ A_ground
6.4 Roof pitch (information)
cos(pitch) = (A_ground − A_flat) ÷ A_slope
6.5 Façade and party wall length (our assumption A1)
3DBAG gives wall areas, not lengths. [ASSUMED A1] façade and party walls have the same average height, so the perimeter is split in the ratio of their areas:
L_facade = P × A_facade ÷ (A_facade + A_party)      L_party = P − L_facade
These lengths are only used for the foundation beams.
7. Step 4 – Floor areas

The gross floor area (BVO – bruto vloeroppervlakte) is the volume divided by our assumed gross storey height (floor to floor) for the profile [ASSUMED A2]. It can never be smaller than the footprint [ASSUMED A16].
BVO = max(A_ground , V ÷ storey height)      Upper floors = BVO − A_ground
Check: usable ÷ gross floor area (GO ÷ BVO) should be 0.6–1.0. If GO is larger than BVO the dwelling unit spans several buildings, so internal walls use min(GO, BVO) [ASSUMED A15].
8. Our own assumptions

3DBAG and BAG measure the size of a building (areas, volume, outline) but not what it is made of or how it is divided inside. Everything in this section fills that gap. None of these values are measured for the individual building; they are our own chosen values for a typical building of that type and age. They can be replaced building by building when better information exists.

blocks.text: 8.2 What is NOT assumed
Footprint, wall and roof areas and volume – measured by 3DBAG from AHN laser height data.
Footprint outline and usable floor area (GO) – from BAG, the Dutch national building register.
Building type and age group – from the input file (material_profile_id).
Perimeter, heights, roof pitch – calculated from the above without any assumption.
8.3 How much each assumption matters (sensitivity)
We changed one assumption at a time and re-ran all 1,082 buildings. The table shows the change in total mass and total CO2 compared with the result in this document (1,800,610 t, 393,535 t CO2e).

head: ID

rows: Concrete floors 25% thinner (e.g. 150 instead of 200 mm)

blocks.text: For mass, concrete floor thickness (A9, -15.2%) and storey height (A2, +8.0%) matter most, because concrete floors are the heaviest part of most buildings. Since 23 September 2026 each reported material group has one flat emission factor, so CO2 now follows mass closely: floor thickness (A9, -11.5%), storey height (A2, +7.7%), installations (A11, ±9.6%) and the amount of reinforcement (A7, ±4.5%) are the largest. The factors themselves (A12) move CO2 one for one.
8.4 Thickness to mass

[ASSUMED A7, A8] Mass per m² = thickness × density. Examples: 100 mm brick = 0.10 × 1,800 = 180 kg/m²; 200 mm reinforced concrete = 0.20 × 2,400 = 480 kg concrete + 0.20 × 80 = 16 kg rebar per m²; 50 mm mineral wool = 0.05 × 30 = 1.5 kg/m².

blocks.text: 8.6 Installations and fixings (all profiles)
[ASSUMED A11] Pipes, wiring, radiators, gutters and fixings are not visible in 3DBAG. We add the same amount per m² gross floor area to every building:
8.7 Emission factors and reporting group

[ASSUMED A12] CO2 released to produce the material (production stage A1–A3). There is one factor per reported material group: every detailed material takes the factor of the group it is reported in, so the CO2 of a group is simply its mass × that factor. All steel together is 85,604 t × 1.55 = 132,686 t CO2e, and all concrete 1,376,665 t × 0.12 = 165,200 t CO2e. Copper has no factor of its own: it is an installation material, so it takes the Other factor 0.50, while still being reported as its own group. These are coarse working values – the same set the earlier estimate used (section 17); for official Dutch reporting they should be replaced with Nationale Milieudatabase (National Environmental Database) values.

9. Step 5 – Component quantities
Each building part has a quantity taken from the measured or derived values:
The kg per unit for every building part is always [ASSUMED A9] (A11 for installations).
Window area = A_facade × window share; closed façade = A_facade − window area.
10. Step 6 – Material mass
mass (kg) = quantity × kg per unit of each layer
The masses of the same material are added over all building parts. Then the 17 detailed materials are grouped into the 7 reported materials:

head: Reported material
Includes
rows: Reinforcement steel, Structural steel, Steel sheet
Aluminium, Zinc / lead, Gypsum blocks, Ceramic roof tiles, Mineral wool, Bitumen roofing, Plastic

blocks.text: 11. Step 7 – CO2
CO2e (kg) = mass (kg) × emission factor (kg CO2e / kg)

CO2 is calculated per detailed material, then added up per reported material and in total. Because every material in a group carries the same factor, the CO2 of a group equals its mass × the group factor (8.7). The output stores mass and CO2 per detailed material in both kg and tonnes.

468 buildings have no flags; together they hold 119,021 t and 26,558 t CO2e.

16. Limits
The build-up is a typical construction per profile, not the actual construction of each building. It can be improved per building with permits, drawings or a site visit.
Floors and party wall thickness drive most of the mass: concrete is the largest material.
Buildings without a storey count (BOUWLAGEN_MISSING) are the least certain.
Foundation piles are not included: at demolition they normally stay in the ground.
Emission factors are one coarse value per reported material group (8.7); replace with Nationale Milieudatabase values for official reporting.
Some notices were matched to a building in a different town than the notice title; the match itself should be checked separately.
17. Comparison with the previous method

The earlier estimate (material_estimation_1081_co2.json, table co2_emission) multiplied the usable floor area (GO) by a fixed kg per m² for each material_profile_id. It did not use the 3DBAG geometry. Both columns below cover the same 1,081 notice buildings; Jan Provostlaan 16 is not in the earlier file.
The previous profiles gave about 2,650 kg per m² for a 1970–2000 house; this method gives about 1,000 kg per m² gross floor area, which fits a Dutch terraced house.
The previous CO2 used 0.5 kg CO2e per kg for sand, gravel and mortar ('overige constructie mineralen'), which made that one group the largest CO2 source.

This method is based on each building's own measured size, so a large building gets more material and a small one less. Both methods now use the same emission factors (8.7), so the whole CO2 difference comes from the material quantities. Both columns cover the same 1,081 notice buildings, so this method reads 1,800,432 t and 393,500 t CO2e here, without Jan Provostlaan 16.
18. How to reproduce
All steps run from the project folder C:\datafuse-ai\dataset:
python geometry_material_co2.py – the single-building worked example (prints every step).
python build_input_1082.py – keeps the 1,081 selected notices, adds Jan Provostlaan 16 (needs internet for PDOK and 3DBAG) and writes 3dbag_input_1082.json.
python geometry_material_co2_batch.py – calculates all 1,082 buildings and writes the JSON and CSV output.
python import_geometry_co2.py – rebuilds the table material_estimation_geometry in database datafuse.
To change an assumption, edit its value at the top of geometry_material_co2_batch.py (PROFILES, INSTALLATIONS, EMISSION_FACTOR, PARTY_WALL_ALLOCATION) and run steps 3 and 4 again.
